title: Dorsal and ventral roots, and where the DRG sits
objective: Place the DRG on the dorsal root and explain the clean sensory/motor separation at the roots.

steps.title: Sensory in the back, motor in the front
steps.body:
At the cord, the two roots are functionally pure:

- the **[[dorsal root]]** carries sensory ([[afferent]]) axons *into* the dorsal (back) side of the cord,
- the **[[ventral root]]** carries motor ([[efferent]]) axons *out* the ventral (front) side.

This back-=-sensory, front-=-motor layout (the Bell–Magendie arrangement) is one of the most reliable rules in neuroanatomy.

steps.title: The DRG rides on the dorsal root
steps.body: The **[[DRG]]** sits as a swelling on the [[dorsal root]], just outside the cord — which fits perfectly: it's the home of sensory cell bodies, and the dorsal root is the sensory entry. The [[ventral root]] has no such ganglion, because its motor cell bodies live *inside* the cord.

steps.prompt: Match each root/structure to its function.
pairs: Sensory cell bodies, on the dorsal root
steps.explanation: Dorsal = sensory in (with the DRG); ventral = motor out. If you know a neuron's cell body is in the DRG, you already know it's sensory.

steps.setup: You cut a single dorsal root (leaving the ventral root intact).
options: Motor output to that segment's muscles
Sensory input from that segment's territory
steps.reveal: Cutting the dorsal root removes sensory input for that segment while motor output (ventral root) is spared — the classic demonstration that the roots are functionally separate.

reviewNotes: Anchors DRG = sensory, on the dorsal root; sets up the neuron's shape.
